planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; the most widely grown cultivar of hardy fuchsia, more compact than the straight species and famously naturalized in hedgerows in the British Isles.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Riccartonii bears the classic hardy fuchsia flower shape, four flared scarlet sepals over four shorter purple petals, on a smaller-flowered, more compact and floriferous plant than the wild species, blooming in profusion from early summer through fall and drawing hummingbirds reliably throughout. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts vigorously from the roots each spring, while in milder zones it stays semi-evergreen. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, since fuchsias in general dislike prolonged high heat; treat as a container plant that can be moved to a cooler, shadier spot during the worst of summer if grown outside its ideal cool-summer range. Mulch the roots heavily going into winter to protect the crown.

common_name: Autumnale Fuchsia (Burning Bush, Bronze-Gold Autumn-Foliage Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; grown primarily for its colorful bronze-gold foliage rather than for vigor.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Autumnale, also sold as Burning Bush, emerges with foliage in shades of bronze, gold, orange, and red that shifts through the season like autumn leaves, a foliage-first fuchsia cultivar that carries the classic red-and-purple pendant flowers as a secondary feature rather than the main attraction. Its colorful leaves make it a useful accent among green-leaved shade perennials even when it is not in bloom. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, since fuchsias in general dislike prolonged high heat and the colored foliage can scorch in strong sun; treat as a container plant that can be moved to a cooler, shadier spot during the worst of summer if grown outside its ideal cool-summer range. Mulch the roots heavily going into winter to protect the crown.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a popular golden-leaved hardy fuchsia awarded the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Genii bears bright chartreuse-gold foliage that holds its color through the growing season, setting off the classic red-sepaled, purple-petaled pendant flowers that appear from early summer into fall and reliably attract hummingbirds. Its compact, well-branched habit and reliable golden color have made it one of the most widely planted foliage-interest hardy fuchsia cultivars. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, since fuchsias in general dislike prolonged high heat and the gold foliage can scorch in strong sun; treat as a container plant that can be moved to a cooler, shadier spot during the worst of summer if grown outside its ideal cool-summer range. Mulch the roots heavily going into winter to protect the crown.

common_name: Voodoo Fuchsia (Large Double Dark Purple-Red Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; a classic large-flowered hanging basket fuchsia rather than a garden-hardy type.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Voodoo bears large, fully double flowers with deep scarlet-red sepals surrounding a mass of dark purple-red petals that appear almost black in low light, one of the most dramatically dark-colored fuchsia cultivars in the trade and a long-time favorite for hanging displays on a shaded porch. Unlike hardy Magellanica-type fuchsias, it has little cold tolerance and is best treated as a warm-season annual or container plant brought under cover before frost. It struggles in prolonged high heat and humidity, so in the Gulf South it performs best in a shaded, breezy spot and may need a summer rest indoors with air conditioning during the hottest weeks. Water frequently, since hanging baskets dry out quickly, and pinch growing tips to encourage a fuller, more floriferous habit.

common_name: Marinka Fuchsia (Historic Trailing Red Hanging Basket Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; a historic trailing fuchsia introduced in 1902 and still one of the most widely grown basket cultivars.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Marinka bears single, deep red flowers with a slightly darker red corolla, trailing readily over the edge of a basket on a vigorous, cascading plant that has remained a favorite for well over a century since its introduction in the early 1900s. Its heavy, reliable bloom and classic trailing habit make it a benchmark red hanging-basket fuchsia against which many newer cultivars are still compared. It has little cold tolerance and struggles in prolonged high heat and humidity, so in the Gulf South it performs best in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering, since hanging baskets dry out quickly; bring it under cover well before the first fall frost.

common_name: Dollar Princess Fuchsia (Historic Compact Double Red-and-Purple Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; introduced in 1912 and still one of the most reliable small-flowered fuchsia cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Dollar Princess bears small, fully double flowers with red sepals over a compact ball of purple-violet petals, a dainty, long-blooming cultivar dating to 1912 that has remained popular for its dense, floriferous habit and its ability to tolerate somewhat more sun and heat than many other fuchsia cultivars. Its compact size and heavy bloom suit a container, hanging basket, or the front of a shaded border, and it attracts hummingbirds reliably through its long summer season. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it still performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, since fuchsias in general dislike prolonged high heat; treat as a container plant that can be moved to a cooler, shadier spot during the worst of summer if grown outside its ideal cool-summer range.

common_name: Tom Thumb Fuchsia (Dwarf Compact Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; one of the most compact hardy fuchsia cultivars, useful for edging or rock gardens.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Tom Thumb bears small red-and-purple pendant flowers typical of hardy fuchsia in miniature, on a dwarf, densely branched plant that stays compact without regular pruning, making it useful for edging a shaded border, tucking into a rock garden, or growing in a smaller container where taller fuchsia cultivars would be out of scale. It flowers heavily from early summer through fall and reliably attracts hummingbirds despite its small stature. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, since fuchsias in general dislike prolonged high heat; treat as a container plant that can be moved to a cooler, shadier spot during the worst of summer if grown outside its ideal cool-summer range. Mulch the roots heavily going into winter to protect the crown.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; a long-established English upright fuchsia cultivar still commonly available.

directions: Grow in a container or shaded bed filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil or potting mix. Display bears single to semi-double flowers with rose-pink sepals over a slightly deeper rose-red corolla on an upright, bushy plant, a long-established English cultivar known for its reliable, heavy bloom and sturdy, self-branching habit that needs less pinching than many other fuchsia cultivars to stay full. It has little cold tolerance and struggles in prolonged high heat and humidity, so in the Gulf South it performs best in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering; bring container plants under cover well before the first fall frost, or treat as a warm-season annual.
